newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin operation tests limits of Kremlin openness.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin operation tests limits of Kremlin openness.

text.p: The Kremlin's record of openness in the run-up to Boris Yeltsin's heart operation had as many ups and downs as the president's health, but its performance on the big day exceeded expectations.
From the moment Itar-Tass news agency announced the start of of the operation 37 minutes after it began, Kremlin spokesmen, doctors and media provided a steady drip of information.

There were no live television pictures of the operation and reporters were kept at arm's length. But it was a far cry from Soviet days when the leader's health was a state secret and his death could go unannounced for two days.

The Kremlin's announcement that the operation had started apparently caught the editors at Russian news agencies off guard. Long used to strict controls from the old days, they refused initially to believe they could run the news.
"I will tease them with this mix-up forever now. They just did not believe me," Kremlin press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters.
Opening a news conference three hours after the operation began, Yastrzhembsky said: "I believe you don't have anything to complain about. We woke you up early enough."
Tass announced the start of the operation at 7.37 a.m. Before it ended seven hours later, Kremlin officials had given several updates on the progress of the operation.
Chief surgeon Renat Akchurin emerged from the operating theatre exhausted but gave a news conference almost immediately. He gave some medical details but drew the line at one point.

"The number of bypasses is much more than the figure (three or four) you mentioned," he said. But he declined to give an exact figure, saying is was up to Yeltsin to decide whether to make this information public.
Even so, Leonid Brezhnev might be turning in his grave. Soviet authorities tried for years to hide the truth about his long illness and took more than two days to announce his death in 1982.

All officials have said Yeltsin's operation went well, although he still faces a delicate recovery period. How the Kremlin and the surgeons would have reacted if the operation had gone badly will remain an open question.
Yeltsin's announcement on state-controlled television on September 5 that he had decided to have a heart operation was a gesture of unprecedented openness by the ruling authorities.
The Kremlin held regular briefings after that at which it gave details of the president's preparations for surgery.

But the Kremlin's new policy of openness highlighted the fact that it had been economical with the truth about Yeltsin's heart for years. It also did not always live up to its promises of transparency about the president's health.
There were many of the "blank spots" which Mikhail Gorbachev used to refer to in history in his drive for "glasnost" (openness) when he was Soviet leader.

The Kremlin refused even to say before the operation when it would start. First news that Yeltsin had blood problems which might complicate surgery, but which were later dealt with, came from doctors or unofficial sources.
Worried that the Kremlin was playing down the risk involved in the operation, Akchurin took it on himself to tell the world that it was not so easy.

He also said that Yeltsin may have had an unannounced third heart attack just before he was reelected in July -- a statement which the Kremlin took unusually long to respond to and explain away as a linguistic misunderstanding.
The Kremlin's vagueness in answering many questions led to much media speculation and attention which Yastrzhembsky had a tough time handling.
"Sometimes I feel like asking you to spare the president, especially the Western media," he said on September 27, sounding a note of frustration.

The openness clearly did not satisfy one Western journalist. A Kremlin official said she tried on the eve of the operation to smuggle herself into the Russian Cardiology Centre where it was carried out but was ejected by security guards.
